interviewQuestions.question: At a high level, how does a text-to-image model like Stable Diffusion work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd walk through it as training vs generation, since that's the cleanest way to explain diffusion. In training, you take a real image, repeatedly add small amounts of noise until it's pure static, and train a network to predict the noise added at each step — so it learns to reverse that process, one denoising step at a time.

At generation time, you start from pure random noise instead of a real image, and run the learned denoising step repeatedly, gradually turning static into a coherent image. To make it text-to-image, a text encoder converts the prompt into an embedding that's fed into the denoising network at every single step, steering each step's noise-removal toward an image consistent with the description — that's why prompt wording has such a strong, granular effect on the output.

I'd mention Stable Diffusion specifically runs this whole process in a compressed **latent space** rather than on raw pixels (latent diffusion), decoding to a full image only at the very end, which is what makes it fast enough to run on consumer hardware.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the forward/reverse noise process clearly, and whether you know where and how text conditioning actually enters the pipeline — not just that it "uses AI to make pictures."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Explaining Stable Diffusion end to end
